title: Approaching population thresholds in presence of uncertainty: Assessing displacement of seabirds from offshore wind farms
abstract: Assessment of the displacement impacts of offshore wind farms on seabirds is impeded by a lack of evidence regarding species-speciﬁc reactions to developed sites and the potential ecological consequences faced by displaced individuals. In this study, we present a method that makes best use of the currently limited understanding of displacement impacts. The combination of a matrix table displaying the full range of potential displacement and mortality levels together with seasonal potential biological removal (PBR) assessments provides a tool that increases conﬁdence in the conclusions of impact assessments. If unrealistic displacement levels and/or mortality rates are required to equal or approach seasonal PBRs, this gives an indication of the likeliness of adverse impacts on the assessed population. This approach is demonstrated by assessing the displacement impacts of an offshore wind farm cluster in the German North Sea on the local common guillemot (Uria aalge) population.

## 1. Introduction

The marine environment is undergoing profound changes (Lange et al., 2010). In addition to a multitude of other anthropogenic uses, the expansion of offshore wind energy installations currently represents the most prominent development in the North Sea (Moksness et al., 2009). The direct impact of offshore wind farms (OWFs) on seabird mortality, e.g. due to collision with rotating blades, is regularly modelled and assessed within impact assessments in several European countries. However, indirect mortality and decreases in productivity as an ecological consequence of displacement from foraging habitats has been neglected until recently, due to the lack of evidence for impact pathways (Furness, 2013; Langton, 2013).

Seabirds show species-specific behavioural responses to operational OWFs. Several species groups show avoidance reactions to OWFs in response to specific stimuli, such as rotating turbines and/or related activities including movements of maintenance/service vessels (Fox and Petersen, 2006). Such behavioural avoidance equates to indirect habitat loss for some species (Furness et al., 2013). The ecological consequences of partial or complete exclusion of birds from the footprints of OWFs and any ‘buffer zones’ around them require careful consideration through environmental impact assessments (EIAs) (Busch et al., 2013; Langton, 2013; Masden et al., 2010a), where potential impacts of displacement have to be assessed based on 2 years of baseline data collected following the application for an OWF (BSH, 2013).

Two key impact pathways are important when considering displacement effects on mobile receptors: the relative strength of the displacement effect (e.g. the percentage of a population relocating as a consequence of a perturbation), and the ecological consequences (e.g. survival and fitness consequences) for the displaced individuals.

In this context, this study aimed to detail a methodology to approach and narrow down the potential effects of marine activities (particularly OWFs) on seabird species by triggering avoidance reactions, resulting in the displacement of individuals from the disturbed area.

We used available evidence on displacement rates and humancaused mortality rates populations can sustain to develop an appropriate method for assessing the biological consequences for seabirds of indirect habitat loss due to displacement from OWFs and their surrounding areas.

Our appreciation of the magnitude of species-specific displacement rates has improved as a result of the increased availability of postconstruction monitoring results (e.g. Vanermen et al., 2012; Percival, 2012; Walls et al., 2012; Leopold et al., 2011; Petersen et al., 2006) and sensitivity indices informed by comprehensive literature reviews (Furness et al., 2013; Garthe and Hüppop, 2004). However, the results still need to be treated with caution because of uncertainties regarding their statistical validity (Furness, 2013) and significance (Maclean et al., 2013). Studies may only indicate whether or not displacement occurs, while species-specific displacement rates remain questionable. Accordingly, more data do not necessarily lead to more reliable results. Focused, post-construction monitoring programmes, involving power analysis to identify a suitable study design, as well as careful timing and appropriate numbers of surveys, are needed to collect data for

single key species and thus help to improve our understanding of the problem. Moreover, population-modelling approaches increase our knowledge of population dynamics and the vulnerability of specific populations to human-caused mortality. The potential biological removal (PBR) approach (Wade, 1998) and other equivalent population models provide tools for assessing the number of additional casualties (above natural background mortality rates) that can be sustained each year by a certain population (Dillingham and Fletcher, 2008).

This study aimed to use the available information as summarised above to address the question of how to assess the biological consequences for displaced individuals, which represents a key parameter in determining the likelihood of a significant negative effect on a specific population. Combining realistic displacement rates with a ‘sustainable harvest rate’ allows the mortality of displaced individuals needed to meet a respective PBR threshold to be derived; if the mortality rate of displaced individuals would need to be unrealistically high, this would argue against a significant negative effect on the population under consideration. However, in light of the above-mentioned uncertainties, the approach developed in this study, rather than providing a definitive answer, aims to allow for more-informed discussion of the potential effects of displacement in the context of OWF approval processes by describing the full range of potential quantitative impacts.

The approach was demonstrated by investigating the potential displacement effects of an OWF cluster in the German North Sea on a common guillemot (Uria aalge) population on the island Helgoland.

## 2. Background

Displacement of seabirds by OWFs may have fitness consequences in terms of likelihood of survival and future reproductive output for both displaced individuals, and individuals that the displaced birds may interact with. Individual fitness may be affected by increased energy expenditure (due to relocating to other foraging grounds) and/or evasion of OWFs resulting in changes to daily energy and time budgets (Masden et al., 2010b), and consequent increases in the costs of average foraging bouts. Individual fitness may also be adversely impacted by reduced rates of energy acquisition if birds have to relocate to alternative and potentially less-profitable feeding grounds, indicating that the strength of any displacement effect will depend on the quality of the habitat that is lost.

Displacement can also have an impact via intensified intra-specific competition for resources within the remaining foraging habitat (e.g. Burton et al., 2006; Durell et al., 2001, 2000), thus potentially increasing the energetic costs of foraging or reducing the rate of energy gain, with possible consequences for individual body condition and reproductive success. OWFs may impact on individuals by any or all of these pathways to increase the mortality or reduce the productivity of bird populations.

The sensitivity of seabird species to displacement might also vary in accordance with specific stages of their annual life cycle, e.g. in relation to breeding, post-breeding or non-breeding seasons.

During the breeding/colony-attendance season, seabirds tend to become central-place foragers, bound to their colonies (Baird, 1991, Burke and Montevecchi, 2009), and are restricted to finding sufficient food within a foraging range, the extent of which is defined by its energetic costs. Accordingly, seabirds may be particularly vulnerable to displacement effects during the breeding season. Ecological theory predicts that breeding adults may buffer their own survival by not attempting to breed or by abandoning breeding efforts when conditions are/become unfavourable (Cairns, 1987; Furness, 2013). This was described by Ylönen et al. (1998) as a trade-off between investments in current breeding and self-maintenance. Long-lived species (Burke and Montevecchi, 2009) like seabirds are generally thought to safeguard their own survival to allow for subsequent breeding attempts in other years (Langton, 2013). Recent studies modelling the effects of displacement of foraging guillemots during the breeding season concluded that

displacement could result in changes to species time/energy budgets, with possible consequences for breeding performance and/or adult survival (Searle et al., 2014). The potential reduction in adult provisioning rates could in turn result in reduced chick growth and survival, and consequently decreased reproductive success (Langton, 2013). Moreover, longer foraging trips may be associated with temporary nonattendance of eggs or young, so increasing the likelihood of failure due to predation or conspecifics (Ashbrook et al., 2008; Ashbrook et al., 2010; Searle et al., 2014). This suggests that unfavourable nutrition during the breeding season may have a greater impact on breeding success than on adult survival (Cairns, 1987). Nevertheless, adult birds that abandon their breeding efforts to secure their own survival, or those reproducing at high individual costs, are likely to suffer from poor body condition by the end of the breeding season (Langton, 2013), and continuation of these fitness implications into the non-breeding season may have knock-on effects for over-winter survival (Erikstad et al., 2009; Harding et al., 2011; NSRAC, 2013). Masden et al. (2010b) suggested that displacement of foraging breeding adults could affect breeding success as well as survival rates. Moreover, the suggestion that colony size may be limited by intra-specific competition for food in the vicinity of colonies during the breeding season (Furness and Birkhead, 1984) highlights the potential ecological consequences of reducing the foraging habitat available to a respective colony.

Although central-place foraging constraints are removed during the non-breeding season, making birds more flexible in terms of habitat choice and thus potentially less vulnerable to displacement from a given area, these considerations may be offset by adverse weather conditions and reduced food availability. The effects of insufficient nutrition and poor body condition during the non-breeding season cannot be mitigated by behavioural changes (e.g. abandoning breeding effort to safeguard own survival), and displacement effects during the nonbreeding season will accordingly impact on individual survival. The mortalities of both juvenile and adult auks seems to be highest during the winter (Furness, 2013), and prey abundance is thought to be the key driver of adult mortality (Mitchell et al., 2004), with contributions from other factors such as pollution and entanglement in fishing gear. However, seabirds will be less restricted in their habitat choice during the non-breeding compared with the breeding season, and may redistribute to alternative habitats at comparably low energetic costs in the absence of the need for regular commutes to a colony. As long as redistribution to an alternative habitat of similar quality is possible, the impacts of displacement may be tolerable, with little or no effect on body condition and survival. The average life span and very low adult mortality of seabirds such as guillemots in an environment characterised by strong fluctuations in prey stocks supports the idea that adult birds can survive periods of below-average prey abundance. However, in a population that is close to carrying capacity, habitat reduction due to displacement could mean that displaced individuals may struggle to find alternative habitats that are not already fully occupied. This situation also has the potential for carry-over effects, as adults unable to find sufficient food during the non-breeding season may not be in adequate body condition to attempt to breed the following spring (Furness, 2013).

A distinct, post-breeding season needs to be considered for several species and species groups, such as auks, seaducks, gannets, and Manx shearwaters. For example, guillemots and razorbills swim away from their colonies in late summer, guiding their flightless chicks into offshore areas and moulting to become flightless themselves during late summer and autumn. Thus although individuals are able to travel further afield than during the breeding season, they cannot cover large distances rapidly, so increasing their vulnerability to displacement if considerable portions of their foraging habitat becomes unavailable and the availability of suitable habitat within range is limited. According to Langton (2013), displacement is unlikely to have an impact if foraging sites can be switched with no effect on foraging efficiency. The ecology of these species indicates the need to consider the post-breeding

season as a distinct period during the annual cycle, during which the impact of displacement may differ from that during other seasons. In addition to auks, other species exhibit distinctive post-breeding behaviours. Juvenile gannets have a period after leaving the nest when they remain flightless (Wernham et al., 2002); Manx shearwaters are reported to concentrate around the Irish Sea front during fledging and early post-breeding (September–October) (Begg and Reid, 1997; Stone et al., 1994; Webb et al., 1990); and seaducks form moulting aggregations post-breeding (Wernham et al., 2002).

Finally, reduced productivity, associated with impeded breeding or increased chick mortality and/or increased adult mortality or reduced survival, has consequences for the population under consideration. While most statements on potential displacement impacts are based on ecological theory and modelling, the above considerations indicate the existence of a complex relationship between prey availability, fitness, reproductive output and survival, with uncertainties regarding the interpretation of the likely ecological consequences. Although potential impact pathways have been identified, e.g. changes in time/ energy budgets with productivity and/or survival implications, there is currently no evidence for the consequences at the individual level. Such relationships are unlikely to be linear, and would be difficult to measure empirically, as noted by Furness (2013).

In this study, assessment of the effects of displacement took a precautionary approach by considering indirect adult mortality rather than reduced reproduction, as requested by nature conservation legislation (Europäische Kommission, 2000) for situations lacking evidence. Moreover, the sizes of bird populations are often defined in the conservation objectives for protected sites (e.g. Special Protection Areas (SPAs)) in terms of breeding pairs, and it may accordingly be preferable to assess impacts via indirect mortality, rather than via the effects on reproductive output.

## 3. Methods

This section describes the methods used as well as the different stages and the evidence informing the assessment process recommended for displacement assessments within Environmental Statements (3.1–3.5). Moreover, the study area, an OWF cluster comprising three OWFs in the vicinity of the island of Helgoland, and the studied seabird population is described (3.6–3.9).

## 3.1. Selection of species for assessment

Sensitivity to displacement differs considerably among seabird species. To suitably focus impact assessment, decision on the most relevant species needs to be made project-specific. The selection of a suitable species will depend on: i) available evidence on species-specific sensitivity, e.g. indices of sensitivity of seabirds to disturbance and/or displacement from habitat (Furness et al., 2013; Garthe and Hüppop, 2004); and ii) abundance/densities at the specific development site (or sites in the case of cumulative or ‘in combination’ assessments).

In the United Kingdom (UK) for example, it is standard practice to identify sensitive receptor species by estimating the population anticipated to occur within the potential impact zone, e.g. those birds displaced within the OWF footprint and surrounding buffer zone. Peak abundance estimates are then compared with thresholds of 1% of various reference populations. Only species with peak abundance estimates N1% of the regional population estimate may be considered as sensitive receptors.

In this context, for species with a significant element of turnover such as species on passage, turnover rates should be taken into account when estimating the overall number of birds passing through an area from which they may be displaced during a certain biological season (e.g. migration).

## 3.2. Displacement levels

Despite an increasing evidence-base for species-specific displacement levels from post-construction monitoring of OWFs, published evidence remains sparse and sometimes contradictory. Low encounter rates of seabird species during site-specific surveys and low numbers of independent samples (survey transects) may impede, or at least compromise, reliable statistical conclusions. Moreover, variability in seabird numbers at any given location reduces the likelihood of detecting changes, even when declines are in excess of 50% (Maclean et al., 2013). Post-construction results thus need to be treated with caution in light of these constraints. In such situations, EIAs should ensure adequate precautions whilst taking account of emerging evidence for better-studied species. For most species, specific sensitivities are best assessed using sensitivity indices as reported by Garthe and Hüppop (2004), and updated and applied to a Scottish context by Furness et al. (2013). For example, the scores for sensitivity to disturbance give a good indication of those species likely to be relevant to a displacement assessment at a specific development site (see Table 1).

## 3.3. Displacement buffers

Seabirds showing avoidance reactions to OWFs may not only be displaced from the footprint of the OWF itself, but also from a buffer zone around the OWF (Busch et al., 2013; Krijgsveld et al., 2010), which thus needs to be included in the assessment. In light of the incomplete and often poor evidence for species-specific displacement distances, we recommend a generic and precautionary displacement buffer distance of 2 km for all species except divers and seaducks, for which a 4-km buffer is recommended, based on evidence for displacement distances (e.g. Percival, 2010; Petersen et al., 2006; Fox and Petersen, 2006) from constructed OWF boundaries.

## 3.4. Matrix approach

We suggest that a matrix approach that relates likely species-specific displacement rates and the associated potential ecological consequences will provide the best assessment and approximation of likely displacement impacts. Although assuming a certain mortality of displaced adult individuals would represent the most straightforward approach in terms of assessment, other consequences of displacement effects, e.g. chick mortality for breeding-season assessments, are also conceivable. In light of the lack of evidence regarding the impact of displacement on demographics, we recommend the assessment of 0–100% displacement and 0–100% mortality (of displaced foraging adults or chicks fed by those foraging adults) to gain an understanding of the overall range of potential displacement-related impacts and to inform discussions on the levels of mortality/reduced reproductive output that might have significant impacts on seabird populations (e.g., aggregations breeding in protected sites such as SPAs required by the EU Birds Directive). This initial assessment should be refined using species-specific evidence to identify a more restricted range of displacement rates, and by simple population modelling using a PBR approach to determine the impacts of different levels of mortality.

A matrix represents a flexible and adjustable tool for presenting the full range of potential displacement levels and potential ecological consequences (Table 2), while allowing the user to indicate their respective interpretations of the most likely impacts e.g. by highlighting cells within the matrix, and providing a full account of the evidence (and its sources) on which that interpretation is based.

## 3.5. PBR approach

The PBR approach (Wade, 1998) is a simple population modelling approach for investigating mortality thresholds of animal populations that can be used to estimate the number of additional casualties (above natural mortality) that a population can sustain each year. Originally developed for the assessment of marine mammals, the PBR approach is now commonly used for ornithological impact

assessments in both marine (e.g. Trinder, 2014) and terrestrial contexts (e.g. Bellebaum et al., 2013). PBR values are thought to support the assessment of the displacement matrix; if only unrealistically high displacement and/or mortality levels in the context of current guidance documents exceed the PBR threshold calculated for a specific population, this would add further certainty to the conclusion that a project would not adversely affect the population under consideration. Nmin represents a conservative estimate of the population size (Dillingham and Fletcher, 2008) and should thus incorporate a ‘measurement error’ inherent in population estimates, as well as an estimate of its degree of uncertainty, suggested by Wade (1998) as the lower bound of a 60% confidence interval, as a precaution to compensate for the lack of data used in the PBR approach. Similarly, colony counts will also include measurement errors (e.g. errors in accurately counting birds present, converting counts to breeding pairs, and inclusion/exclusion of non-breeders associated with the colony), which should be estimated and incorporated (Dillingham pers. comm., October 20, 2014). These errors may be represented by the coefficient of variance (CV). A conservative CV of e.g. 0.25 corresponding to an error of ±25% may be advisable, but lower CVs have been used in some assessments (e.g. assessments for the UK Triton Knoll and Hornsea Project 1 OWFs), and the decision needs to be made at a project-specific level, depending on the quality of the available population data.

The third key parameter is the recovery factor f, which is an arbitrary factor reflecting the level of concern about the population under consideration that can be used to implement alternative management strategies (Dillingham and Fletcher, 2008). Dillingham and Fletcher (2008) advised the use of the following f values, according to IUCN population status level, in the absence of project-specific population conservation goals (e.g. due to the requirement to maintain or increase a specific SPA population): f = 0.1 for all threatened species, f = 0.3 for nearthreatened species, and 0.5 for species of least concern.

It is important to note that impact assessments often consider only one source of human-caused mortality, e.g. potential indirect mortality from OWF developments (single-source mortality). Total and seasonal PBR estimates thus need to be interpreted in this context and may have to allow for factors other than OWFs, which may cause casualties. If a PBR value is not achieved based on the single-mortality risk being considered, the inclusion of other potential causes of mortality may still indicate potentially unsustainable mortality. This must be taken into account when considering any conclusions drawn from assessments focusing on single-pressure/mortality risks. Zydelis et al. (2009) highlighted the fact that PBR estimates apply not to single-source mortality, but to additive mortality. At the same time mortality from OWF developments may represent the single most important new, immediate risk faced by many seabird species. Further sources of humancaused mortality (e.g. by-catch, oil pollution etc.) may have been present for longer periods, and may, at least to a certain degree, already be reflected in the adult survival rates used to derive the maximum recruitment rate (Rmax).

If applied with the necessary caution, the PBR approach is an appropriate tool for informing decision-making about protected sites and populations given that it tends to make safe, albeit conservative, management recommendations in the face of minimal data (Dillingham pers. comm., October 20, 2014).

## 3.6. Study area

Fig. 1. Case study area.

The island and surrounding sea are protected by two designated SPAs, the Seabird Protection Area Helgoland comprising the breeding cliffs of Helgoland and marine areas around the island, and the Eastern German Bight comprising marine areas to the north of Helgoland (Fig. 1).

An OWF cluster is located north-west of Helgoland within the foraging range of the guillemot population breeding on the island. The cluster – comprises the three OWFs Meerwind Süd/Ost (~24 28 km), Nordsee – – Ost (~30 35 km) and Amrumbank West (~35 40 km) (Fig. 1).

Although the OWFs themselves are situated just outside the SPAs, the 2-km displacement buffer zone of one OWF overlaps with the Eastern German Bight SPA. The guillemots breeding on Helgoland are qualifying features of the SPA and the population is afforded protection at the breeding site and in the designated marine areas adjacent to Helgoland. ‘Off-site’ impacts on SPA populations that are temporally remote from the breeding season and/or spatially remote from the breeding site also need to be assessed, given that SPA populations are afforded protection throughout the year (JNCC and Natural England, 2013a).

Three or four bio-seasons are traditionally described for auk species such as guillemots: the breeding season, the post-breeding season/dispersal, the non-breeding season, and spring migration (e.g. Garthe et al., 2007).

For the purpose of this assessment, we suggest using the term ‘colony-attendance season’ instead of breeding season, because adult birds are bound to their colony well before the start of egg-laying. According to Dierschke et al. (2011), guillemots visit their breeding cliffs at Helgoland from October onwards. Their presence then becomes more pronounced in January and February and regular in March, while egglaying starts during the first half of April. After hatching in May, most chicks jump off the breeding cliffs in mid-June, with a mean jumping date between 2000 and 2009 of 18th June. Male guillemots than accompany their chicks out to sea, and most are reported from the sea west of Helgoland in July. Most adult female guillemots remain at the colony until the end of June, and only occasional chicks and female adults are present on the breeding cliffs during July (Dierschke et al., 2011). The colony-attendance season was thus defined as the period from March to the end of June.

A post-breeding season when moulting flightless adult guillemots and their still flightless chicks are found on the sea in the vicinity of their breeding colony also needs to be assessed. Because they are flightless, the birds are unable to travel large distances and/or change location rapidly, making them more vulnerable to displacement at this time than during the subsequent non-breeding season. Based on the German Sea Birds at Sea database (1990–2006), Markones et al. (2010) recorded virtually no flying guillemots (0.7%) in the German North Sea between 16th July and 30th September. Accordingly, the post-breeding season has been defined as the period from July to the end of September.

The period between the post-breeding and colony-attendance seasons (October to the end of February) was considered as the non-breeding season in this assessment. Although a fourth season (e.g. spring migration) can be defined for many species, the guillemot subspecies (U. aalge albionis) that breeds on Helgoland, in Britain south of c. 55°38'N, and in Ireland, Brittany and western Iberia (Sangster et al., 2011) shows no distinctive migration pattern, unlike the subspecies U. aalge aalge that breeds in northern Europe. Although ties to their colony diminish during this season, adult guillemots remain in waters close to their breeding colony all year around (Mendel et al., 2008). Ringing recoveries of British guillemots demonstrated a median recovery distance from colonies of 357 km for adults during winter (Wernham et al., 2002). In the case of Helgoland, it is likely that most 3rd year and older birds stay in the southern and eastern North Sea during the winter (Nettleship and Birkhead, 1985, Hüppop and Hüppop, 2009).

but it was unclear if those birds were related to the colony or represented non-breeders. Mendel et al. (2008) reported low to medium densities within a radius of about 30 km around Helgoland in the summer.

The Helgoland guillemot population is relatively isolated, with the closest colonies in the UK and Norway, thus increasing the likelihood that birds in the vicinity of the island during the colony-attendance and post-breeding seasons can be associated with that colony.

It has been suggested that colony size and the extent of foraging flights are interlinked variables. On average, birds from smaller colonies have more restricted foraging ranges, probably as a result of less density-dependent competition for food (Wakefield et al., 2013, Lewis et al., 2001, Furness and Birkhead, 1984). However, environmental variables and prey distribution are likely to have a greater effect on foraging range than colony size.

To accommodate the precautionary principle and in accordance with UK statutory interim advice (JNCC and Natural England, 2013b), the mean maximum foraging range of the study species, as given by Thaxter et al. (2012), should be considered when assessing the potential displacement effects of developments for the duration of the speciesspecific colony-attendance season.

Based on general and colony-specific guillemot foraging ranges, we considered birds occurring within the Helgoland OWF cluster during the colony-attendance season to be linked to the local colony. In addition to an overlap between the mean maximum (84.2 km) and mean foraging range (37.8 km) (Thaxter et al., 2012) and all three OWFs considered, the lack of other colonies with a foraging range within these OWFs supported an association between the observed birds and the Helgoland colony. The three OWFs considered represent the only OWFs that overlapped with the mean foraging range for guillemots according to Thaxter et al. (2012). Colony-specific information on foraging ranges indicated that the foraging range of Helgoland breeding birds was restricted compared with larger colonies, and OWFs within the mean maximum foraging distance according to Thaxter et al. (2012) were therefore not considered.

When applying the suggested approach to projects in the vicinity of multiple colonies, we recommend apportioning the guillemot population observed within the development footprint and its buffer zone to the colonies within foraging range based on colony size and distance from the assessed OWF.

The isolation of the Helgoland colony supports the assessment that guillemots recorded in the OWF cluster during the post-breeding season were also related to that colony.

## 3.9.1. Abundance data

## 3.8. Foraging range

Foraging range, i.e. the distance adult birds travel during the colonyattendance season in search of food for themselves and their offspring, is commonly considered in EIA studies to relate birds recorded foraging at sea to specific colonies. In a recent review of 25 seabird species by Thaxter et al. (2012), guillemot was among the three species for which there was the highest degree of confidence in relation to the identified foraging range. Based on direct tracking studies, the study estimated a mean foraging range of 37.8 km (±32.3) and a mean maximum foraging range of 84.2 km (±50.1), with a maximum recorded foraging range of 135 km.

In terms of colony-specific information for Helgoland, Dierschke et al. (2004) reported a concentration of guillemots within a 15–20km radius of the island, extending to about 40 km in northern, western and south-eastern directions during the chick-rearing period, based on – ship-transect surveys (1990 2003). A single aerial survey (2003) recorded most guillemots within 5 km of Helgoland and low densities up to about 25 km from the island. The furthest observations were made 43 km north, and 69 km and 83 km north-west of Helgoland,

Abundance data used for the assessment have been taken from environmental impact assessment studies focusing on the third investigation year prior to construction for the respective OWFs (Piper et al., 2012, Braasch et al., 2011, Schuchardt et al., 2011).

## 3.9.2. Reference populations

Three reference populations were derived for the respective bioseasons. Abundance data for the considered OWFs were available for 2010–2012. There were 2872 breeding pairs of guillemots (Dierschke et al., 2012), equivalent to 5744 breeding adults, in the colonyattendance season in 2011, and this was taken as the reference value. Breeding adults are more restricted in their foraging ranges than non-breeders attending the colony, making breeders more vulnerable to displacement impacts and thus implying that assessments should focus on breeding adults. However, the estimate of potentially displaced birds during the colony-attendance season therefore needs to be corrected for the presence of non-breeders. According to Grunsky-Schöneberg (1998) non-breeders represent about one third of the population (see also Table 6).

For the post-breeding season, non-breeding adults and immature birds associated with the colony, in addition to breeding adults, were included in the reference population. Like the breeding adults, these birds undergo moult and become highly vulnerable during this period. Grunsky-Schöneberg (1998) reported that the proportion of nonbreeders associated with the colony was almost constant, and estimated proportions of two thirds breeders and one third non-breeders. We accordingly used a reference population of 7,659 guillemots (5744 + (5744/3)) for this season in our assessment. The isolated location of the colony makes it unlikely that larger numbers of guillemots from other colonies would occur in the vicinity of Helgoland during this period, and no influx of birds from other colonies was therefore considered.

For the non-breeding season, the German mid-winter population, reported as 33,000 individuals (Garthe et al., 2007), was used as the reference population.

## 4. Results

## 4.1. PBR analysis

A theoretical maximum growth rate λmax for guillemots was estimated based on age of first reproduction and adult survival (Niel and Lebreton, 2005). Guillemots are deferred breeders and normally start reproducing at 5 years (Mendel et al., 2008). An adult survival value of 0.946 was used based on a long-term study from Scotland (Harris et al., 2000).

For the purpose of this assessment, we used an f value of 0.3, consistent with advice on suitable f values for healthy protected populations (Dillingham pers. comm., October 20, 2014). PBR values based on f = 0.3 were taken forward to assessment, but values derived using less and more precautionary f values are also presented in Table 5 for comparison.

A measurement error of 25% and the lower bound of a 60% confidence interval were used to derive Nmin. This appeared to be an appropriate level of error based on using a colony-specific conversion factor (Dierschke et al., 2011) to estimate the number of breeding pairs, based on a count of adults on land (Dierschke et al., 2011).

The mid-winter guillemot population (33,000 individuals, Garthe et al., 2007) represents an estimate based on extrapolation from surveys with limited coverage. As above, a 25% error and the lower bound of a 60% confidence interval were used to reflect the uncertainty of the population estimate (see Table 4 for a summary of parameters for PBR analysis).

Season-specific PBR values were calculated to allow for seasonspecific assessment. This represents an OWF-focused assessment approach (i.e. whether the assessed OWF cluster has the potential to have an unsustainable impact on the population during the respective season) rather than a population-focused assessment (where the overall year-round impacts on a specific population are considered).

As shown in Table 5, the risk that seasonal PBR values are met (being smaller, proportionally to exposure time) is considerably higher than assuming the respective seasonal pressures would be constant throughout the year, in which case impacts would be assessed against the total PBR. This is because seasonal PBR values allow for mortalities outside the season assessed, as well as for mortalities from other causes, which may be more dominant during other seasons.

## 4.2. Displacement assessment results

Assessment of the abundance data estimates that the three OWFs in the Helgoland cluster cumulatively have the potential to affect 146 guillemots during the colony-attendance season, of which an estimated 97 are likely to be breeding adults. Table 6 provides an overview on the individual and cumulative displacement potentials of the assessed OWFs for each bio-season.

Entering displacement values for individual or combined OWFs into the displacement matrix allows their detailed assessment, as shown in Table 7.

The specific combination of displacement and mortality values taken forward to assessment in EIA and/or habitat regulation assessment (HRA) studies should be based on the latest available speciesspecific evidence. The current exemplary assessment considered guillemot displacement rates of 70% (Bligh OWF, Belgium (Vanermen et al., 2012)) and 50% (Egmond aan Zee and Princess Amalia OWFs, The Netherlands (Leopold et al., 2011)) in more detail, given that significant displacement has been reported from these sites according to some surveys. However, indications of lower guillemot displacement rates have been reported from other sites (e.g. 30% at Robin Rigg OWF, Scotland, Walls et al., 2012; 26% at Thanet OWF, England, Percival, 2012; Horns Rev. OWF, Denmark, Petersen et al., 2006).

Theoretically, 100% displacement and mortality of the displaced birds would result in the loss of all individuals likely to make use of the area during this period, while 70% displacement and 10% mortality during the colony-attendance season would lead to 7 casualties, and 50% displacement and 10% mortality would result in the loss of 5 individuals (Table 7a). Although the appropriateness of using 10% mortality in assessments is unclear, given the lack of evidence, UK statutory nature conservation bodies (SNCBs) have advised the use of 10% mortality (JNCC advice to Rhiannon OWF, Stage 2 PEI, May 2014) as a conservative estimate based on expert opinion, or a range of 1–10% mortality (Natural England, 2014) for guillemots in the interim. In contrast, developers have claimed that 1% or 2% mortality is more appropriate, also based on no clear evidence. In this context, it should be highlighted, that mortalities are likely to correlate strongly with the quality of the habitat lost; if key foraging habitat is lost and the remaining habitat is already close to carrying capacity, then the mortality rates of displaced birds may be considerably higher than 10%.

## 4.2.1. Colony-attendance season

For the 2011 guillemot breeding population, a seasonal PBR of 20 individuals was derived for the colony-attendance season (Table 5). The displacement matrix indicates that at 70% displacement, 30% of the displaced birds would have to suffer from mortality to reach the seasonal PBR, while at 50% displacement, the seasonal PBR would be reached at 40% mortality. If all displaced guillemots died, then only about 20% displacement would equal the seasonal PBR (Table 7a).

## 4.2.2. Post-breeding season

For all adult and immature guillemots (excluding juveniles) associated with the colony in 2011, a seasonal PBR of 20 individuals was derived for the post-breeding season (Table 5). Considering the same displacement rates, about 18% mortality at 70% displacement, or 24% mortality at 50% displacement would be required to reach the seasonal PBR. If all displaced guillemots died, then displacement of about 12% would achieve the seasonal PBR (Table 7b).

## 4.2.3. Non-breeding season

Considering the much larger German North Sea mid-winter guillemot population during the non-breeding season, the seasonal PBR of 141 individuals (Table 5) would be reached at approximately 65% mortality and 70% displacement, 92% mortality and 50% displacement, or 100% mortality and 46% displacement (Table 7c).

## 5. Discussion

The application of the methodology presented in this study will help to increase confidence in displacement assessments based on limited, but best-available evidence at that point in time. Although there is considerable potential for further improvements in displacement assessments through directed research addressing specific evidence gaps (e.g. summarised in Busch et al. (2015)), the outlined approach allows for an immediate consideration of displacement effects within the framework of impact assessments.

In addition to the highlighted need for further research into realistic displacement and mortality rates, the different impacts of displacement on breeding adults and non-breeding (adult or immature) birds during the colony-attendance season, and season-specific variations in the ecological consequences of displacement also need to be addressed to improve the reliability of displacement assessments, as also indicated by e.g. Furness (2013) and Langton (2013).

The appropriateness of assessing mortality impacts against seasonal or total PBR values needs to be considered. The use of seasonal PBR values does not allow simple conclusions to be drawn regarding the likelihood of a specific population declining as a result of humancaused impacts, given that this would need to take account of the total annual sustainable take, i.e. total PBR. However, seasonal assessments better reflect specific threats that vary according to seasonal parameters, such as the size of the reference population and its spatial flexibility (e.g. bound to colony or far-ranging). Acknowledging the considerable uncertainties involved in displacement studies, seasonal assessments may thus represent one of few options for concretisation of results.

Moreover, further consideration is needed to determine if displacement impacts are likely to represent an ongoing, year-on-year effect, increasing annual mortality rates of a respective seabird population during every year of the operational period of an OWF, or if seabird populations might adapt to the extent of the remaining foraging habitat over time. In the latter scenario, displacement may represent a one-off effect leading to a smaller but stable population size, where, after a phase of adoption, displacement may not continue to generate the same level of impacts each year (Busch et al., 2015).

The results of the case study indicate that the currently outlined Helgoland OWF cluster, not accounting for any other potential sources of human-caused mortality, is unlikely to have a significant effect on either the Helgoland guillemot population or the wider, non-breedingseason population. During the colony-attendance and post-breeding seasons when guillemots are most restricted in their habitat choice and may therefore be most vulnerable, unrealistically high mortality rates (18–30%) would need to occur to equal the calculated seasonal PBR value, even considering a potentially precautionary 70% displacement effect. Significant effects of the Helgoland cluster alone during the nonbreeding season can also be ruled out, considering that a mortality of approximately 65% of displaced birds (at 70% displacement) would be required to reach the seasonal PBR, which seems unrealistic.

However, the results suggest that the OWFs will have a clear impact on the local guillemot population. While apparently not at levels deemed unsustainable in the context of EIA or HRA assessments, because of forcing the local population into decline, considerable proportions of the seasonal PBR values during the colony-attendance and post-breeding seasons may be ‘used up’, assuming realistic displacement rates and relatively low mortality rates. For example, a quarter of the seasonal PBR for the colony-attendance season would be accounted for by 50% displacement and 10% mortality, and a third of the seasonal PBR by 70% displacement and 10% mortality. During the post-breeding season, 60% displacement and 10% mortality would use up half the seasonal PBR. This suggests that further wind farm developments within the foraging range of the Helgoland colony could relatively fast reach a point where unsustainable impacts through displacement could not be safely precluded, especially if areas close to the colony, which support relatively high densities of guillemots, are developed. Furthermore, as noted above, additive mortality due to other causes during the respective season also need to be accommodated within the seasonal PBR.

The results of the assessment for the non-breeding season are not surprising, given the dilution of the potential displacement effects of the Helgoland cluster over a larger area (German North Sea). While only the impact of OWFs within the foraging range of the colony needs to be considered during the colony-attendance season, the seasonal PBR for the non-breeding season will have to accommodate an undefined number of potential casualties from further OWFs within the German North Sea. It should be noted that all the assessments in this study should ideally take account of other potential sources of humancaused mortality. A cumulative impact assessment at the German North Sea scale should therefore be carried out to assess the realistic impact of potential OWF displacement on the German North Sea midwinter guillemot population.

Assessing the cumulative impacts of bird/wind farm interactions represents a major challenge (Masden et al., 2010a). In this context, the results of this case study indicate the need for cumulative displacement assessments to be informed by season-specific distribution and activity patterns. As highlighted throughout this paper, there are many uncertainties inherent in any assessment, and several assumptions need to be made when approaching this issue. However, the comparison of a range of displacement and mortality rates with seasonal PBR values allows a better evaluation of the risks that specific seabird populations face in relation to OWF projects.

## 6. Conclusions

This paper publishes the displacement matrix approach, used in several recent OWF applications in the UK, in a scientific journal and further enhanced this approach by linking it with PBR analysis.

The introduced displacement assessment approach represents a novel tool for providing further insight into this impact category. We provide a step-by-step description of the assessment process and apply it to a specific case. This detailed account of the process will

support EIA practitioners assigned to carry out such assessments within the framework of OWF approval processes.

Given the uncertainty surrounding several key parameters defining the strength of displacement effects, the presented methodology does not prevent, but makes the best use of the currently incomplete available knowledge. The full range of potential impacts is presented in the displacement matrix to inform discussions, while consideration of current knowledge on displacement rates and the use of seasonal PBR values allows us to determine the level of mortality that needs to be achieved to have a significant impact on a seabird population during species-specific seasons. The likelihood of reaching the mortality rate required to meet the respective seasonal PBR will need to be assessed based on expert knowledge. Nevertheless, this analysis will allow for better-informed decision-making based on the likely magnitude of displacement effects in a range of situations, thus increasing confidence in the conclusions of the assessments.

Displacement assessments are likely to become more accurate with the increasing availability of evidence, and the approach detailed here, i.e., the combination of a displacement matrix with PBR, appears fit for purpose. However, there is an urgent need for more empirical data on the consequences of displacement to allow further refinement of the assessment tools in light of more evidence becoming available.

The results of the current case study indicate that the combination of a displacement matrix with season-specific PBR values allows for confident conclusions about the potential effects of displacement to be drawn. Regarding the Helgoland guillemot population, the results indicate that cumulative displacement associated with the current level of OWF development within the birds' foraging range is unlikely to have an unsustainable effect on the population during the seasons assessed. However, it was also found that individuals of the population will be affected, and the scope for additional impacts from further OWF developments in the vicinity of the colony or any other human-induces pressures on the population is thus limited without considerably increasing the risk of adverse impacts on this protected seabird population.

Malte Busch received his diploma in Environmental Science from University of Lüneburg in 2009. He worked for several years at the Institute for Coastal Research at the Helmholtz Centre Geesthacht, being involved in national and international projects investigating the environmental impacts of offshore wind farm development. After moving to the UK to work for two years as Environmental Specialist for marine ornithology at the English statutory nature conservation Natural England, providing advice on marine infrastructural developments, he returned to Germany where he started his PhD at the University of Kiel and works as a self-employed consultant.

Stefan Garthe studied Biology at Hamburg and Kiel University. In 1997 he earned his doctorate in Zoology studying seabirds in the North Sea. From 1997 to 2000 he had a postdoc position at the Institute of Marine Science in Kiel, followed by an Assistant Professorship at the Research and Technology Centre (FTZ), in Büsum. In 2007, he became a senior scientist at the FT Z and was appointed professor at Kiel University in 2014. Since 2004, he is also Adjunct Professor at Memorial University of Newfoundland in St. John's, Canada. Since 2013, he is the president of the German Ornithologists' Society.
